title: [2025] SHSC 1
text:
In the St Helena Supreme Court                                                                                                   1/2025 

                                                                                                                        

 Between 

   

 AG 

   

 -v- 

   

 Alan Lawrence 

   

  

 Sentence 13 th March 2026 

  

   

 Section 93 of the Welfare of Children Ordinance 2008 & Section 1 Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 1992 apply to this ruling. Nothing may be published if it is likely or calculated to lead members of the public to identify any complainant or person under 18 involved in these proceedings 

   

   

 1.       Mr Lawrence you were found guilty after trial of the offences of buggery, indecent assault and gross indecency with a child. The indictment period starts on the 25 th of June 1978 and ends on the 26 th of June 1982 for the buggery and indecent assault and the 26 th of June 1980 for the gross indecency. These dates represent the victim's 16 th and 14 th birthdays respectively. The evidence at trial suggested that these offences occurred before you went to Ascension in 1980. 

 2.       You were born on the 29 th of December 1961. In 1978 you would have been 16 years old and in 1979 17 years old. Your victim would have been 12, 13 or 14 at the time he was abused by you. For the purposes of sentencing you I will take your age at the time of the offences as having been in the 16 to 17 year old age bracket as the evidence, and the jury's verdict on the gross indecency matter, would place you at about that age. I will refer to your victim as AB. 

   

 Approach to Sentencing 

   

 3.       I will approach sentencing in this way. I will treat you as having been under 18 but older than 15 at the time you offended. The guidelines issued by the sentencing council on sentencing historical sexual offences at paragraph 9 suggests the following approach: 

   

 If the oﬀender was very young and immature at the time of the offence, depending on the circumstances of the offence, this may be regarded as mitigation affecting the offender's culpability. Further, where the offender was under 18 at the time of the oﬀence the court must consider the principles set out at paragraphs 6.1 to 6.3 of the Sentencing Children and Young People guideline. The court should take as its starting point the sentence likely to have been imposed at the time of the offending, and bear in mind the maximum sentence which could then have been imposed on the child offender. 

   

   

 4.       Paragraphs 6.1 to 6.3 of the guideline on sentencing children and young people provides: 

   

 6.1 There will be occasions when an increase in the age of a child or young person will result in the maximum sentence on the date of the finding of guilt being greater than that available on the date on which the offence was committed (primarily turning 12, 15 or 18 years old). 

   

 6.2 In such situations the court should take as its starting point the sentence likely to have been imposed on the date at which the offence was committed. This includes young people who attain the age of 18 between the commission and the finding of guilt of the offence but when this occurs the purpose of sentencing adult offenders has to be taken into account, which is: 

   

 the punishment of offenders; 

 the reduction of crime (including its reduction by deterrence); 

 the reform and rehabilitation of offenders; 

 the protection of the public; and 

 the making of reparation by offenders to persons aﬀected by their offences. 

   

 6.3 When any significant age threshold is passed it will rarely be appropriate that a more severe sentence than the maximum that the court could have imposed at the time the offence was committed should be imposed. However, a sentence at or close to that maximum may be appropriate. 

   

 5.       Although in St Helena law there is no threshold as to differing sentences available when an offender becomes 18, either now or in 1978, but it has always been widely acknowledged that when it comes to sentencing young people under 18 a differing approach needs to be taken to have regard to the offender's youth. I will therefore treat you as having passed a significant age threshold between the time you offended and the time of your sentencing, while taking into account the purpose of sentencing adult offenders. 

 6.       When having regard to the starting point for sentence it is right that the guidance for imposing custodial sentences on young people contained within paragraphs 6.42 to 6.49 of the guideline on sentencing children and young people is also had regard to in addition to the purpose for sentencing adult offenders. It would be an impossible task for any sentencer in 2026 to assess what a court would have actually imposed in 1978 or 1979. 

 7.       The guidance issued by the sentencing council for sentencing children and young people will also be had regard to. Of importance is the following extract: 

   

 Where a custodial sentence is unavoidable the length of custody imposed must be the shortest commensurate with the seriousness of the offence. The court may want to consider the equivalent adult guideline in order to determine the appropriate length of the sentence. 

   

 If considering the adult guideline, the court may feel it appropriate to apply a sentence broadly within the region of half to two thirds of the appropriate adult sentence for those aged 15 - 17 and allow a greater reduction for those aged under 15. This is only a rough guide and must not be applied mechanistically. The individual factors relating to the offence and the child or young person are of the greatest importance and may present good reason to impose a sentence outside of this range. 

   

 8.       I will also have regard to the appropriate adult guidelines when considering the appropriate sentence. 

   

 The Offences 

   

 9.       The victim in this case was the child of a lady who you worked with at the Old People's Home. You already knew her before you started working there and you lived close by. When she would work a night shift from 8pm to 8am you would babysit AB, and at times his sister who was 2 years younger. You would share a bedroom with AB when you stayed over. 

 10.    AB recalls that you took him into the outside toilet where you sat on the toilet and masturbated while you had him stand in front of you exposing his genitals to you, this is the gross indecency with a child matter. He also recalls being in the bedroom that you shared with him and you placing his penis in your mouth, that being the indecent assault, and also you had him squat over you while you penetrated his anus with your penis, this being the buggery. The verdict of the jury requires that I sentence you on the basis that each event occurred just once. The evidence may also support the conclusion that the offence of indecent assault occurred on the same occasion as the buggery. 

 

 Other Matters 

   

 11.    I have received a victim statement that speaks of the impact of this offending upon AB. He has struggled with relationships, has trouble trusting people and feels angry, frustrated, sad, unfulfilled and misunderstood. His alcohol intake is also high which is no doubt a coping mechanism. This type of reaction is all too common in this type of offending and it is reflected in the sentencing guidelines. 

 12.    Two very helpful sentencing notes were prepared by counsel for which I thank them. I have considered these along with the submissions made to me today. 

 13.    There is an application for a restraining order on conviction. I cannot make this order as St Helena law only permits it for offences contrary to the Protection from Harassment Act 1997. This is a matter I have sought to bring to the attention of the Attorney General through numerous previous Crown Counsel to no avail. To my mind victims of sexual offenders deserve protection from their abusers, unfortunately this is not available on St Helena by the making of a restraining order on conviction. 

 14.    I have received a pre-sentence report that suggests that you may have cognitive deficits. I note that you pose a low risk of reoffending but that if you were to reoffend the risk of harm would be high. I also accept what is said in the report about your vulnerabilities and ability to cope in a custodial setting. 

 15.    I also have received a number of character references that speak very highly of you, including one from your employer. It is clear that you have worked all your life caring for others and do so with dedication. 

 16.    What is also clear is that given that you have had no convictions in your life up until this point that what went on with you and AB does not reflect the individual you became in later life. I say this not to diminish or excuse what you have done but by way of acceptance that the man I have to sentence is a more mature version of the young person who committed these incredibly serious offences. 

   

 Applying the Guidelines 

 

 17.    For the buggery the correct guideline to use is that for sexual activity with a child. I do not use the rape guideline as the jury did not have to consider consent and on the evidence of the complainant (which touched on this point very briefly, could be seen as ambiguous and was untested) I have doubt on that issue. Combine that with the fact that AB could well have been over 12 years old I consider it would be inappropriate to use the rape guideline. Buggery of a boy under 16 carries a maximum sentence of life imprisonment and sexual activity with a child carries 14 years for an adult, or 5 years for those under 18 as you were. 

 18.    Harm is in category 1 as it involved penetration of the anus. 

 19.    Culpability is high as there was a clear abuse of trust. You had a significant level of responsibility towards a child in that you were there to care for and ensure that no harm came to him, this was not a one off arrangement but one that went on for about a year for 2 to 3 nights a week for 12 hours at a time. 

 20.    I see no evidence that AB was targeted because he was particularly vulnerable, he was vulnerable by virtue of his age and that you were in charge of him but that does not make him particularly vulnerable. Nor can I find, in the absence of a conviction or admission, that AB was particularly vulnerable due to having been abused by another man before you abused him. 

 21.    I therefore do not accept the prosecution assertion that AB was particularly vulnerable simply because he was a child in your care. Nor is there anything to suggest that you specifically targeted AB because of his vulnerabilities. 

 22.    For an adult offender this provides a starting point of 5 years' custody with a range of 4 to 10 years. 

 23.    In relation to aggravating factors I cannot find that the offence occurring within the victim's home is an aggravating factor, it has already been taken into account by the finding of an abuse of trust due to you being a babysitter. 

 24.    In relation to mitigating factors there is your vulnerability in a custodial setting, your lack of previous convictions and your positive good character since the commission of the offences. 

 25.    If you had committed the offence as an adult I would impose a sentence of 4 years' imprisonment. 

 26.    For the indecent assault the correct guidelines are those for sexual activity with a child. These are guidelines predicated on a maximum sentence of 14 years' custody. Where the offender is under 18, as you were, the maximum is 5 years. The maximum for indecent assault was 10 years. This involved penile penetration of the mouth placing harm in category 1 and culpability in category A due to the abuse of trust. This provides a starting point of 5 years custody with a range of 4 to 10 years. Similarly to the buggery there are no aggravating factors and the same mitigating factors apply. 

 27.    If you had committed the offence as an adult I would impose a sentence of 4 years' imprisonment, even allowing for the differing maximum penalties between indecent assault and sexual activity with a child. 

 28.    In relation to the gross indecency with a child the correct guidelines are those for engaging in sexual activity in the presence of a child. The maximum sentence for that offence is 10 years' custody, or 5 years for those under 18. For gross indecency with a child it is 2 years for the period covered by this indictment. The offence involved masturbation and an abuse of trust placing the offence in category 2A with a starting point of 2 years' custody with a range of 1 to 3 years. With no aggravating factors and the same mitigation as for the buggery, and applying a measured approach to the guidelines having regard to the differing maximum sentences, had you been an adult the appropriate sentence would have been 12 months' custody. 

 29.    If I sentenced you today as having committed the offences as an adult the indecent assault and buggery offences would run concurrently as they may have occurred on the same occasion making a total of 4 years' imprisonment. The gross indecency with a child sentence would run consecutively as it would have occurred on a separate occasion and it is necessary to mark the fact that the abuse was not a one off but repeated itself. This would provide a total of 5 years' custody. 

 30.    Taking account of totality the sentence for gross indecency with a child would be reduced by 6 months making a sentence of 4 years and 6 months' custody. 

   

 The Sentence 

   

 31.    I now consider the impact on that sentence of your age at the time of offending and the passage of time between the offending and the date of sentence. To my mind these two factors can properly be reflected by imposing a sentence of 50% of that I would have imposed had you committed the offences more recently as an adult. 

 32.    This provides a total sentence of 2 years and 3 months' imprisonment. Making an allowance of 15% for prison conditions this provides a total sentence of 23 months imprisonment. 

 33.    The sentences are therefore: 

   

 Buggery (ct. 5)                                      21 months' imprisonment 

 Indecent Assault (ct.1)                           21 months' imprisonment concurrent to the sentence for buggery 

 Gross Indecency with a child (ct. 3)        2 months' imprisonment consecutive to the sentence for buggery 

   

 34.    The offences are too serious not to be marked with an immediate custodial sentence and so I cannot suspend the sentence or impose a non-custodial sentence. The sentence is therefore one of 23 months' immediate custody. 

   

   

   

   

   

   

 Duncan Cooke 

 Acting Judge of the Supreme Court 

   

 Dated: 13 th March 2026 

   

   

   

 NB - this sentence was considered by the Court of Appeal on an appeal by the Attorney General. The appeal was dismissed. The relevant reference is AG v Lawrence [2026] SHCA 2/2026

title: [2026] SHSC 6
text:
SHSC 06/25 & 36/25 

 In the St Helena Supreme Court 

   

 Between 

 Attorney General 

   

 -v- 

   

 Andre Thomas 

  

 Sentence 13 th of February 2026 

  

   

 Section 93 of the Welfare of Children Ordinance 2008 & Section 1 Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 1992 apply to this ruling. Nothing may be published if it is likely or calculated to lead members of the public to identify any complainant or person under 18 involved in these proceedings 
 

   

   

 1.       Mr Thomas you are to be sentenced for a number of offences. These are: 

 i.                   Taking 236 indecent images of a child in category B between the 4 th of December 2004 and the 8 th of February 2005 

 ii.                  Taking 151 indecent images of a child in category C between the 4 th of December 2004 and the 8 th of February 2005 

 iii.                Possessing 835 indecent images of a child in category A on the 12 th of October 2024 

 iv.                Possessing 172 indecent images of a child in category B on the 12 th of October 2024 

 v.                 Possessing 11,871 indecent images of a child in category C on the 12 th of October 2024 

   

 2.       The last three offences took place on Ascension and the first 2 on St Helena. 

 3.       For the St Helena offences the victim was 14 years of age and known to you. It is clear that on multiple occasions over 2 months you took photographs of him in your bedroom. Some of these showed the boy naked with an erection, an adult hand holding his penis and there are photographs of the boy after he had ejaculated. On occasion the boy looks distressed. 

 4.       At the time these images were taken you would have been 44 years old, so 30 years older than your victim. The images were discovered with the Ascension Island material stored on hard disc drives and depict multiple incidents of sexual abuse of the boy during which you were present.  

 5.       The Ascension offences involve a significant number of images of many different victims, some of which are moving images. Some of the victims were every young indeed, including images of those as young as 4 to 6 months old being penetrated anally by adult males. Most victims were pre-pubescent, some were babies or toddlers and many of them appeared distressed, or in pain, or both. What you possessed were images of the worst type of sexual abuse and you clearly possessed them over a considerable period of time. 

 6.       I do not accept that it is right to categorise this offence as being one where I can take into account that the category A images represented a small amount of the overall number of images. I come to this conclusion based upon there being 835 images, the very young ages of the victims and the extremity of the abuse depicted. 

 7.       The suggestion that you made in your pre-sentence report that you never looked at the images is not one I can accept. You kept them locked in a safe and the images were stored on usb sticks and dvds. When asked for the combination to the safe you refused to provide it. Additionally some images were described and catalogued on an excel spreadsheet recording the ages of the children in the images and what those images depicted. This indicates clearly that you knew what you possessed, that the images were illegal and that you deliberately stored them on removable media to aid you in hiding them. 

 8.       I do not hold your minimisation of the offences against you, it is difficult for people to come to terms with having committed these types of offences. I can only urge you to take part in the Horizon intervention programme to assist you in future and to prevent repetition of similar offending. 

 9.       I also make it clear that I do not find any element of concealment within the meaning of the guidelines or grooming. 

 10.   I have had regard to the pre-sentence report and all that has been so ably said on your behalf. 

 11.   Turning to the St Helena offences I will take the category B matter as the lead offence for sentencing. The starting point for that sentence is 2 years. The victim was known to you and this was not a single photograph but a significant number of images taken on differing occasions over a period of time where the boy at times appeared distressed. Having regard to your lack of relevant previous convictions I consider the appropriate sentence is one of 30 months' imprisonment which is reduced to 24 months to reflect your late guilty plea, for which I have allowed 20%. 

 12.   For the category C offences the starting point is 18 months' imprisonment and having regard to the same matters I have considered when coming to the sentence for the category B offences I consider the appropriate sentence is 24 months' custody, this is reduced to 19 months having regard to your guilty plea. These sentences will run concurrently to one another making a total of 24 months' imprisonment. 

 13.   Turning to the Ascension offences the category A offence will attract the longest sentence. There is a starting point of one year's custody but the offences are significantly aggravated by the very young age of some of the victims, the distress and/or pain exhibited by them and the large number of different victims. The guidelines make it clear that significant weight should be given to the age of the victims and even taking into account your lack of previous convictions the appropriate custodial sentence is one of 30 months which is reduced to 20 months due to your early guilty plea. 

 14.   For the category B offences the number of images were less and I am not told the age of the victims or if any distress shown by them. In light of this the sentence will be one of 26 weeks' custody reduced to 17 weeks to run concurrently to the category A offences. The category C offences start at 3 months' custody are reduced to 2 months, again to run concurrently making a total of 20 months for the Ascension matters. 

 15.   These two sets of offences represent offending at differing times and it is appropriate that the sentences run consecutively to one another making a total of 44 months. 

 16.   I now consider totality and reduce the total sentence to 40 months. I then apply a further discount of 15% to reflect prison conditions. Reducing the sentence to 34 months. After discussion with your counsel you are aware that this does bring you within a differing release regime but I am invited to apply the full 15% which I do. 

 17.   This sentence is too long to suspend and the offences are too serious to consider a non-custodial option. 

 18.   The sentences are: 

   

 i.                   The category B St Helena offence 20 months' custody 

 ii.                  The category C St Helena offence 19 months' custody, concurrent to the category B St Helena matter 

 iii.                The category A Ascension offence 14 months' custody consecutive to the St Helena offences 

 iv.                The category B Ascension offence 17 weeks' custody concurrent to the category A Ascension matter, but consecutive to the St Helena offences 

 v.                 The category C Ascension offence 2 months' custody concurrent to the category A and B Ascension matters, but consecutive to the St Helena offences 

 vi.                Total 34 months' custody 

   

 19.   All USB sticks, CDs, laptops, hard disc drives, DVDs, VHS cassettes, cameras and any other digital media devices capable of storing data seized by the police are to be forfeited and destroyed after 12 months of this order. 

 20.   There will be a sex offenders prevention order until further order in the terms as already discussed. You will also remain subject to the notification requirements for an indefinite period. 

   


   

 Duncan Cooke 

 Acting Judge of the Supreme Court 

   

 13 th of February 2026

title: [2026] SHSC 1
text:
In the St Helena Supreme Court sitting on Ascension                                                  SHSC 1/2026                      

   

 Between 

   

 AG 

   

 -v- 

   

 Mudaliyar Ramachandran 

   

  

 Sentencing 18 th March 2026 

  
 

   

   
 Mr Ramachandran you have pleaded guilty at the first opportunity to an offence of wounding contrary to section 20 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861. You entered a not guilty plea to an offence contrary to section 18 of the same legislation and I formally record a not guilty verdict in relation to that, the Attorney General having offered no evidence. 
 On the 18 th of December 2025 at the Residency you were employed as a cook along with Mr Kuttapan at a Christmas function. Also employed at the function was Mr Malairaja who is your friend. During the time that you were working you would go to the bar and drink whisky and beer which was free of charge. Both Mr Malairaja and Mr Kuttapan continually advised you to stop drinking but you ignored them. 
 As the event wore on you became more drunk and you got upset at Mr Malairaja as you believed that he had not catered sufficiently for the staff at the function. You told Mr Malairaja that you were in charge and slapped him to his left cheek, in response you were slapped back. 
 You then picked up a wine glass, smashed one end onto a table to break it and attempted to push it into Mr Malairaja's face. As Mr Malairaja raised his hand to defend himself the glass cut his left middle finger. You then attempted to stab Mr Malairaja in the face again with the broken glass but the blow was deflected. However on the third attempt you struck Mr Malairaja to the left side of the head with the glass causing a laceration. After this you had to be separated and the police and an ambulance were called. 
 Mr Malairaja had 3 lacerations, 2 to the scalp which were stapled and one to the finger which was sutured. The lacerations to the scalp were 2 cm each and the one to the finger 3cm.  Mr Malairaja did not want to make a formal complaint against you as you are friends but did provide a witness statement. 
 I take from your pre-sentence report that although you sought to minimise what you did you recognise you should have walked away and that you are thankful that there is no lasting injury to your friend. 
 I note that you tend to work overseas for the US forces to support your family in India and that you are currently unable to support them as you have lost your employment over this. I further note that you are a qualified plumber but are now likely not to be able to work for the US forces again. In light of this not only will you suffer for some time because of your actions, but your family will as well. 
 I have received two very helpful sentencing notes which I will have regard to. I have also received a reference, 3 certificates and a verification of employment that speak to your good conduct in the work environment. 
 Turning to the guidelines there was the use of a weapon which places culpability in category B, I do not consider that a broken glass can be described as a highly dangerous weapon having regard to the extent of harm that would normally be expected from a broken glass. It might cause some disfigurement or at the very worse the loss of an eye if used in a particular way which makes it a dangerous weapon, but it is not one that can be described as being substantially above and beyond the legislative definition of an oﬀensive weapon. Highly dangerous requires something over and above dangerous, for example a knife of some length or a firearm, both of which can cause very significant harm or death with little effort on the part of the user. 
 Nor do I accept that the assault was persistent, on the evidence this was an incident where the violence was over quickly and could not be said to have gone on for some time, certainly not long enough to permit a persistent assault to have occurred. It is right that only two attempts to inflict harm may be described as persistent in some circumstances, but to my mind it would be unfair to make that finding in your case where there was a short lived struggle. I also note that you have been convicted of a s.20 offence as opposed to a s.18 matter. 
 Harm was thankfully minor in terms of this type of offence and has left no lasting impact upon Mr Malairaja placing it in category 3. 
 This provides a starting point of 12 months' custody with a range of a high level community order to 2 years' custody. This was an offence committed while under the influence of alcohol when you were seeking to berate your friend which aggravates the offence. It is suggested that there were children at the party and the presence of a man dressed as Santa Claus would suggest that was the case. The purpose of treating children being present as an aggravating factor is to reflect the psychological harm that may be caused to those who witnessed the offence, and in the absence of any evidence that children did in fact witness what occurred I cannot find that this aggravates the offence. 
 You do however have no previous convictions and a positive good character. I will not vary from the starting point of 12 months' custody. This court has always allowed a one third discount for a guilty plea at the plea and case management stage and you will be allowed that amount of credit for your guilty plea, this reduces the sentence to 34 weeks' custody. With a further reduction for prison conditions that is 29 weeks' custody. 
 I look to see if there is a meaningful non-custodial option available and there is not. Ascension cannot accommodate probation or community service orders and in any event you will lose your right of abode after today. I now consider if the sentence can be suspended. Your actions could have caused significant life changing injuries to your friend, stabbing someone to the face can cause disfigurement or even loss of sight. However set against this I believe that your risk of reconviction is low given your lack of previous convictions and age, you will lose the ability to support your family if incarcerated and you would be in a foreign jail where you do not speak the language. 
 In light of this I am just minded to suspend the sentence. The sentence will be one of 29 weeks' custody suspended for 2 years. The impact of this is that you will not go to prison today but if you commit an imprisonable offence in the next 2 years this sentence can be activated alongside any additional punishment you may receive for the new offence. 
 You have no money so I make no order for costs or compensation. 


   

   

   

   

 Duncan Cooke 

 Acting Judge of the Supreme Court 

   

 18 th March 2026

title: [2026] SHSC 7
text:
In the St Helena Supreme Court                                                                             SHSC 7/2026                                                                       

 Between 

   

 AG 

   

 -v- 

   

 Warren Benjamin 

   

   

   

 Sentence 29.5.26 

   

   

   

 1.      Mr Benjamin you are to be sentenced today for one offence of assault by beating and one of harassment. Offences of common assault and perverting the course of justice to which you have entered not guilty pleas will lie on file. 

 2.      Your victim in both offences was your then partner Terri Francis. The assault occurred in the home after you had been looking at her phone and questioned her about the name of a man you had found. She left you to go into another room and you followed her. As part of an altercation between the two of you, you assaulted her. You say that this was done recklessly and you will be sentenced on that basis but I note in your pre-sentence report you claim you acted in self defence, which does not reflect your basis. Whatever the circumstances you clearly used some force as your victim went to hospital the next day due to a sore neck causing very tight muscles which required pain relief. Not only that but she was forced to leave her own home and go into the refuge. 

 3.      Three days after the assault, and when she was in the refuge, you harassed her. You arranged for your sister to deliver a telephone to the refuge which you rang over 10 times in 80 minutes. You also texted her a number of times which included asking her to drop the charges against you. I treat this offence as particularly serious as after you assaulted her and forced her to leave her own home you then deliberately set out to undermine the purpose of the refuge with no thought as to the impact on your victim. She was observed after you called her to be very frightened, worried and distressed by what you did. 

 4.      The pre-sentence report indicates that you clearly have little understanding of the impact of your behaviour and limited empathy for your victim. You know very well the seriousness of what you have done as you have been before the court before for behaving in a similar way and been punished for it. 

 5.      Turning to the guidelines on the assault I will place culpability in category B. The assault caused more than minor physical harm in the context of common assault. This brings you within category 1B on the guidelines with a starting point of a medium level community order. 

 6.      The matter is aggravated by your previous convictions, that it was committed in a domestic context and your victim was forced to leave her own home. I find no mitigating factors. In light of this the appropriate penalty in your case is a term of imprisonment for 12 weeks. With credit for plea of 1/3 that is 8 weeks' custody. 

 7.      In relation to the harassment there was a high degree of planning in that you obtained a telephone and tricked your sister into delivering it, this places culpability in category A. Your victim was described as very frightened, worried or distressed which I consider to be serious distress falling just short of very serious distress but above some distress. I therefore place this in category A2 at the upper end and will take as a starting point 10 weeks' custody. 

 8.      Your previous convictions aggravate the matter, as do the facts that the offence occurred within a refuge where Miss Francis should have been safe and you were also on bail for the assault. I find no mitigating factors. The appropriate penalty is one of 15 weeks' custody. With credit for plea that is 10 weeks' custody. 

 9.      These offences occurred on differing days and the sentences should run consecutively, providing a sentence of 18 weeks' imprisonment. I have considered totality and consider that this sentence properly reflects the totality of your offending. I make no allowance for prison conditions at this stage. 

 10.   I now need to turn to whether there is a meaningful non-custodial option available or failing that whether the sentence can be suspended. 

 11.   I agree with the assessment that you pose a medium risk of serious harm to Miss Francis and that risk must extend to any new relationships you might form. I would be justified in finding that a probation order would not have any meaningful impact on you. Your insight into your behaviour is poor and you lack empathy. Your previous conviction for domestic violence should have been a wake up call that you cannot offend in this way, yet you chose to do so. The harassment took place 3 days after you assaulted Miss Francis and was clearly planned which indicates that you are quite prepared to offend in this way if you think you can get away with it. 

 12.   However I believe that the best hope for those you are in intimate relationships with is to impose a probation order of 2½ years as a direct alternative to a prison sentence of 18 weeks. This order is aimed at reducing the risk you pose to women through domestic violence and will include a condition that you undertake 100 hours of unpaid work to prevent recurrence of like offences by way of deterrence. 

 13.   The impact of the order being a direct alternative to custody is that should you breach the terms of the order, or offend during the period of it, then you are likely to go to prison for 18 weeks in addition to any other punishment that may be imposed at the time. 

 14.   Understand? 

 15.   Explain impact of probation order. 

 16.   Consent? 

 17.   Due to the risk of harm that you pose to your victim it is necessary for this court to protect her from you to prevent recurrence of this type of offending. There will be a restraining order as follows: You are prohibited from contacting directly or indirectly Terri Francis for a period of 2 years. Should you breach that order this court can impose a prison sentence of up to 5 years. 

   

   

   

             Duncan Cooke 

             Acting Judge of the Supreme Court 

   

             29 th of May 2026

title: [2026] SHSC 5A
text:
In the Supreme Court of St Helena                                                                                  5/2026 

   

 AG 

 -v- 

 Keegan Thomas 

   

 Ruling after Trial 

   

 1.      This is a ruling after trial in relation to Keegan Thomas who elected to be tried by a judge alone. 

 2.      Mr Thomas faces allegations of assault occasioning actual bodily harm ('ABH') and false imprisonment. Both allegations are said to have occurred on the 27 th of December 2025 and the complainant in both matters is Rebecca Caesar-Crowie with whom Mr Thomas was, prior to that date, in a relationship with. 

 3.      I will reach my verdicts on the evidence that I have heard in this courtroom and take into account the submissions made to me. I do not have to decide every disputed point that has been raised in the trial, only those that are necessary for me to reach my verdicts. 

 4.      Some points are not disputed. The evidence that was read to me and given in the form of admissions or agreed facts is not in dispute. But on other points I have heard different accounts from different witnesses. 

 5.      Where there is conflicting evidence, I must decide how reliable, honest and accurate each witness is. When doing this I will apply the same fair standards to all witnesses, whether they were called for the prosecution or for the defence. Just because the defendant comes from the dock to give his evidence does not make his evidence any less reliable, and I will judge his evidence by the same fair standards as any other witness. 

 6.      I may draw sensible conclusions from the evidence I have heard, but I must not guess or speculate about anything that was not covered by the evidence. I will guard against emotion, sympathy or disapproval. 

 7.      I will summarise the evidence in this ruling but just because I have omitted something in the summary does not mean it will not be taken into account and, likewise, if it is included it does not mean that I find it to be relevant. 

 8.      The complainant in this matter gave evidence by way of a pre-recorded ABE interview and was cross-examined via a live link. This is perfectly normal in criminal proceedings and cannot be held against the defendant. 

 9.      Other witnesses gave evidence via live link because they were overseas and their evidence, like that of the complainant, is treated in the same way as that of a witness who was present in court. 

 10.   I direct myself on the law as follows: 

   

 Legal Directions 

   

 Burden and Standard of Proof 

 11.   The prosecution must prove that the defendant is guilty. The defendant does not have to prove anything to me. The defendant does not have to prove that he is innocent. The prosecution will only succeed in proving that the defendant is guilty if I have been made sure of his guilt. 

 12.   If, after considering all of the evidence, I am sure that the defendant is guilty, my verdict must be ' Guilty ' . If I am not sure that the defendant is guilty, my verdict must be ' Not Guilty ' . 

   

 Separate Verdicts 

 13.   I will consider each count separately and return separate verdicts on each count. My verdict does not have to be the same for each count. 

 

 The Indictment 

 Assault Occasioning Actual Bodily Harm. 

 14.   The indictment is made up of two counts. The first is an assault occasioning actual bodily harm, contrary to section 47 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861. The particulars allege that Mr Thomas on the 27 th day of December 2025 assaulted Rebecca Caesar Crowie by beating her, thereby causing her actual bodily harm. 

 15.   An assault means the use or threat of unlawful force against another and by including the words 'by beating' the prosecution makes it clear that the assault involves the application of force to the body of Miss Caesar Crowie. 

 16.   Unlawful means that there is no legal justification for the use of the force, for example self defence 

 17.   The use of the force must be either intentional or reckless. There are no circumstances in this case where the offence could be said to have occurred recklessly and I do not need to address that 

 18.   The assault must occasion, or cause, actual bodily harm. Actual bodily harm is any injury calculated to interfere with the health or comfort of the victim. 

 False Imprisonment 

 19.   The second count on the indictment alleges an offence of false imprisonment contrary to common law. The particulars allege that Mr Thomas on the 27th day of December 2025 falsely imprisoned Rebecca Caesar Crowie and detained the said Rebecca Caesar Crowie against her will. 

 20.   False imprisonment consists of the unlawful and intentional or reckless restraint of a  person's freedom of movement from a particular place. It is unlawful detention which stops the person from moving away as they would wish to move.  There is no requirement for there to be a use or threat of force to effect the restraint of the person's freedom of movement. 

 21.   Unlawful means that there is no legal justification, for example acting under the authority of a court order or arresting someone in accordance with the law. 

 22.   As for the ABH allegation, the issue of recklessness does not arise in this case. 

   

 Bad Character 

 23.   I have admitted the fact and facts of the following previous convictions of the defendant, common assault in 2013, common assault in 2019, common assault in 2022, common assault in 2023 and common assault in 2025 only so far as those convictions relate to Bertina Benjamin, a previous partner of the defendant. These have been reduced to admissions. 

 24.   The prosecution say that the convicitons show that Mr Thomas has a tendency to commit offences of this type and so it is more likely that Mr Thomas intentionally assaulted Miss Caesar Crowie at Seaview and detained her against her will thereafter. 

 25.   The defence say that the previous convictions relate to a different partner and do not show that Mr Thomas has a tendency to act as alleged against Rebecca Caesar Crowie. 

 26.   My ruling on the admissibility of the evidence outlines the purpose to which the evidence may be put and I remind myself of that ruling. 

 27.   I must not convict Mr Thomas wholly or mainly because of the previous convictions. The fact that someone has offended in the way alleged in the past does not prove that he did so on this occasion. Mr Thomas' previous convictions may only be used as some support for the prosecution case if, having assessed the evidence, I am satisfied that it is right so to do. 

   

 Complaint Evidence 

 

 28.   As part of the prosecution evidence there is some evidence of the complainant's distress when she returned home and as part of that some limited evidence was led as to what she said. The evidence of what was said cannot further the prosecution case as it is not independent evidence, it simply establishes why the complainant's mother behaved in a certain way and why she paid attention to the injuries she saw on her daughter. 

   

 The Evidence 

 29.   I turn now to consider the evidence that was received. The first evidence was that of Rebecca Caesar Crowie. Her evidence in chief was given by way of a pre-recorded video designed to achieve best evidence ('ABE'). 

 30.   With the consent of the parties I have had a copy of the transcript of the ABE throughout these proceedings. However I paid particular attention to the evidence as it was being played and observed the witness during it. I have also made a very careful note of the cross-examination and when remining myself of what the witness said on any one point I will pay as much regard to what was said during cross-examination as the evidence in chief. 

 31.   Miss Caesar Crowie started by saying that she had been at the seaside on the evening of the 26th to 27th of December 2025. She had gone out with her brother and Thiery to her stepfather's birthday party. Her stepfather is called Donny and her mother is called Melanie. 

 32.   She describes driving home in the car with Keegan driving and her in the front passenger seat, her brother and Thierry were in the back seats. She described that the car started acting up so she got out of the car and started walking down the road. She said that Keegan chased her and she got punched to the face a couple of times. She remembers blood coming down, her crying and asking to go home. 

 33.   She said she doesn't know what happened to her brother and said that she had been drinking. After she had been punched she just spaced out. She does though remember crying, asking to go home and Keegan telling her no. 

 34.   She remembered getting back into the car and being driven to Longwood. She said the more that she asked to get out of the car the more he wouldn't stop. Even when she tried to open the door to get out of the car he would reach over and hold her back. 

 35.   She remembers wanting to go to her house and Keegan driving straight past it. Keegan drove her to her uncle Jeremy's house. She said that when she tried to run away he would grab her and tell her not to go anywhere. She said he just kept attempting to hit her every time she wanted to go or move. He even attempted to hit her when she was in the toilet. She said that he followed her around the house and that she was crying. 

 36.   She described being like a prisoner and him not letting her go anywhere. She said that he was just more concerned with controlling her and her just staying there. She has her own room at Jeremy's so she went to it and he followed her there. When she closed the door he was trying to bust it down. She says she laid down and he was just hovering, and when she did try to get up he laid directly on top of her. 

 37.   She said she was in a lot of pain and couldn't move her mouth properly. She said she cried herself to sleep and when she got up in the morning there was blood everywhere. She said her mother then rang her and she drove to her mother's, she took Keegan with her as she just wanted to get rid of him. On the journey she told him that she wanted nothing more to do with him and he pulled up the handbrake. When he did that she got out of the car and started walking back down the road but he wouldn't let her walk back home. She said she got back in the car and as soon as the car got to her house she ran inside. 

 38.   Once inside she told her mother what Keegan had done, and her mother called for the police. 

 39.   She was asked further about the evening. She said she finished work at about 10:30, went to Kayleigh's house to have a wash before going out to meet her brother, her mother and Donny. When she got to Donny's she met her brother straight away and then spoke to Donny, her mum, Thierry and her brother, who is called Mickshane. When Donny's closed her group went to the seaside to get in her car. She said that Keegan was with them as he was driving her car that night. 

 40.   On the journey home he wasn't speaking and then he just started screaming at her. She was asked how drunk she was and she said that on a scale of 0 to 10 she was at 7 or 8. As the car got to Seaview it started acting up and it was then that Keegan shouted at her saying there was something wrong with the car and that she didn't listen. 

 41.   At this point she tried to get out of the car and she was thinking that if she went back into town they could get into Mickshane's car and he would take them home, however Keegan just pulled her back when she started walking down the hill.  He then tried to put her in the car, then he hit her which led to blood pouring down her face. She confirmed that she was hit with a clenched fist, she can remember his hand coming into her face when she was in the passenger seat and he was in the driver's seat. The punch happened after she got back into the car because he dragged her back into it. She did not know where Mickshane or Thierry had gone. 

 42.   The injuries were to her nose and her top lip. 

 43.   After he hit her the car started and then they drove by her house but he wouldn't stop there, instead he drove to Jeremy's house. When they arrived she opened the door and got out and Mr Thomas was right behind her following her. She kept telling him that she wanted to go home and she said to herself that the only way to not get hurt was to do what he told her to do. At the house she pushed against the front door but the glass broke and that is when she cut her arm. She describes that when she was inside the house she couldn't do anything, and she was crying to go home. Whenever she said that she wanted to go home he would just, in her words, attempt to hit her. By that she described him making a threatening motion as if to pounce on her, or raising his arm to make her scared. 

 44.   She said that her mother rang Keegan's phone the next morning because she had left her own phone at Kayleigh's house. As they were driving home she describes him pulling up the handbrake, so she left the car, got out and walked back down the road. However, he wouldn't even let her do that so she got back in the car and once they got to her's she got out of the car and ran home. 

 45.   Miss Caesar Crowie confirmed that the contents of her ABE interview were true. She looked at some photographs within the trial bundle and said they were taken by Andre Bak on the 27th of December 2025. She described what the images showed. 

 46.   Mr. Dawson who represents Mr. Thomas then asked a number of questions. She confirmed that the tyre on her car had burst on the 26th of December 2025. She had asked Mr. Thomas to get her a new tyre which he agreed to do. Because she did not have a car she had to walk to work, she started at 4 pm. She said she didn't tell the police about being with Keegan when the tyre burst because she didn't want to get into trouble for being around him. 

 47.   She was asked where her daughter was that weekend, and she said she wasn't sure if she was with her sister or another family member, but she knew that she had plans for Lahna to stay with somebody else. She denied planning to stay with Mr. Thomas that night. 

 48.   It had though been arranged that Mr Thomas would bring the car into town that evening. The plan was that he would collect her after work and they would then go out. Her clothes for that evening would have been in Mr. Thomas's car. She accepts that she would have called Mr. Thomas, but she can't say if she asked him to bring a bottle of wine with him. 

 49.   In relation to the wine she says she can't recall drinking any in the car after work but accepts that she probably did have a drink whilst in the car. She confirms that she went to Kayleigh's house but cannot say how long she was there. She was then driven to Donny's bar but doesn't know what time she arrived there, probably 10 past or ¼ past 11. 

 50.   Donny's closes at 1.15 and she left when it finished, she clarified though that she wasn't sure what time Donny's closed on that particular evening. She agrees that she drank alcohol in Donny's, that would have been drinks and shots. She does disagree with the assertion that she was drunk, she can still remember what happened and she was still focused on what she had to do. She says that she only felt 'foggy' after Keegan had hit her. 

 51.   After Donny's they went to the sea front. However, they were not there for long, no more than an hour. 

 52.   She disputes that she had agreed to remain with Keegan that evening. She described the journey home, agreeing that the music was quite loud in the car. When there was a problem with the car Keegan shouted at her, Mickshane and Thierry were in the car at that time. She does not remember saying to Keegan that she wanted to drive the car. When the car stopped she got out of it and walked down the road towards town. She disputed releasing the handbrake to cause the car to roll down the hill at that stage. She said that happened after Mr. Thomas had come after her, she said she interfered with the handbrake during the altercation with Mr. Thomas as she was angry. 

 53.   As she got out of the car and started to walk away Mickshane and Thierry followed her. Keegan chased after her but Mickshane and Thierry had gone by the time Mr. Thomas had got her back into the car. 

 54.   She said that the intention was for all of them to go and get Mickshane's car, she did not choose to stay with Mr. Thomas at that stage. She said she doesn't recall helping Mr. Thomas turn the car around. She does though remember going up the road in the car and asking Mr. Thomas to take her home. She said that she had not arranged to stay at Jeremy's that evening with Mr. Thomas. As they drove past her house she tried to jump out of the car as she was trying to get away from Mr. Thomas and go home. She accepts that she probably did retaliate against Mr. Thomas as he sped up. She did this to get him to stop the car. She says she didn't know where she was hitting Mr. Thomas and doesn't recall grabbing the steering wheel or him grabbing her by the wrist. When asked whether it was a possibility that she did grab the steering wheel or grab him by the wrist she said no it was not. 

 55.   She said it was not at this stage that there was contact with her mouth, that happened before the car started at Seaview, and not while Mr. Thomas was driving the car. She clarified that the assault occurred inside the vehicle but it was not as a result of him protecting both of them whilst driving. 

 56.   At Jeremy's the car was parked close to the house and she walked towards it. Mr. Thomas got out and stood behind her, she disputes that he was putting the windows up on the car while she walked towards the house, saying that she didn't arrive at the property before Mr. Thomas. She described how her arm went through the glass door and disputed that she fell on to the door. She said she didn't have a choice to go to hospital at that stage to get her arm seen to. She said she was crying for Mr. Thomas to let her go home and she had no freedom of movement within the property as he was following her about the house. 

 57.   When she went into the bedroom the door does have a latch and you need to use a key or a knife to open the door from the outside. Mr. Thomas tried to break the door down after she closed the door and latched it. 

 58.   She says that when she went to sleep Mr. Thomas was sat on the bed because he didn't want her to leave 

 59.   When she woke up she heard Mr. Thomas' phone ringing and it was her mother. Mr. Thomas passed the phone to her after he had answered it. She spoke to her mother at that stage. She didn't tell her mother that Mr. Thomas was holding her against her will, she didn't say that because Mr. Thomas was there at the time. She simply told her mother where she was and that she was coming home. 

 60.   She drove home and took Mr. Thomas with her as he was going to go to the woods. At one point Mr. Thomas pulled on the handbrake during the journey and so she got out of the car and walked away. 

 61.   Once at her own home she got out the car and went into her house and Mr. Thomas remained in the car on the road. 

 62.   She clarified at the end of cross examination that she was held against her will in the car on the way to Jeremy's and she was held against her will whilst at that house. She also clarified that he did assault her prior to starting to drive from Seaview. 

 63.   Miss Evans for the prosecution then ask some more questions. Miss Caesar Crowie clarified that her house is in Deadwood and Jeremy's house is just seven houses along on the same road. She confirmed that she was assaulted when she was in Seaview. She also confirmed that she did try to jump out of the car near her own home and said that she could see that she may have had contact with Mr. Thomas at that point. 

 64.   She said that during the journey she was crying, upset and scared and wanted to be home. She recalls shouting out for her mother in the car. She said that when Lahna is not at home Mr. Thomas can come and stay at her house, so had she planned to spend the night with Mr. Thomas it would have been there. She also had plans the next morning to decorate the house for Donny's birthday. 

 65.   Melanie Caesar Crowie then gave evidence. She is the mother of Rebecca Caesar Crowie. She lives at Deadwood with Rebecca, Lahna and her husband. On the night of the 26th to 27th of December she went into town and later got home at about 12.30 to 1.00 in the morning. She did see Mr. Thomas that evening along with Rebecca when she was at Donny's. Rebecca and Keegan were still there when she left. 

 66.   The next morning was when she next had contact with her daughter. Rebecca was not in her room and she was expecting her to be there. She tried to phone her, but there was no answer. She then discovered Keegan's phone number on the house phone and she called that at 9 am. 

 67.   Rebecca then came home. She noticed at first that Rebecca's eyes were puffy and she asked her what was wrong with her. They spoke and she then looked at her daughter a bit longer. She noticed that Rebecca's eyes and mouth was swollen, there were scars across her breast, her arm was cut and one side of her face was puffy. Rebecca was angry and upset. 

 68.   In light of this she went to confront Mr. Thomas who was sat in the car at the top of the driveway. She said that she was raging and angry because of what Rebecca had told her. Mr. Thomas denied hitting Rebecca and said that he had put his arm across her to stop her jumping out of the car. That made her more angry and an argument ensued. 

 69.   After Keegan had left she went back indoors. She spoke further with Rebecca and as a consequence of this she telephoned the police. Rebecca hugged her and cried on her shoulder, and she noticed how swollen her nose was. 

 70.   Mr Dawson then asked some questions. She said that she doesn't know what arrangements Rebecca and Keegan had made for the evening. She confirmed that when she called Keegan he answered and he volunteered that Rebecca was with him and he handed the phone to her. 

 71.   She confirmed that when she was speaking to Mr. Thomas outside the house that he had said that he didn't hit Rebecca. She was asked if he had told her that Rebecca had grabbed the steering wheel and she disputed this, saying that he simply said that he had put his arm out to stop her getting out of the car. Mr. Thomas left after having pulled all the leads out of the ignition to the car. 

 72.   Mickshane Caesar Crowie was the next witness to give evidence. He is Rebecca's elder brother and knows Keegan because he was did dating his sister. In December 2025 he was on a Saint Helena. He was at Donny's on the night of the 26th to 27th of January for the birthday celebration. He confirms that he saw Rebecca at Donny's but isn't sure whether he saw Keegan or not. After Donny's he was at the landing steps. There were quite a few people there including Rebecca, Keegan and Thierry. 

 73.   He had no plan for how he would get home that evening so arranged to hitch a ride with Rebecca and Keegan. He describes driving in the car, Keegan was the driver, Rebecca the front passenger and him and Thierry were in the back. 

 74.   He describes how the car cut out at Seaview and then Keegan started shouting something about the car. When Keegan was shouting he was annoyed at Rebecca. As the argument progressed he and Thierry started walking towards Longwood. Keegan and Rebecca had got out of the car before them and they were also walking in the direction of Longwood, 10 to 15 metres ahead. 

 75.   He saw Keegan then push or throw Rebecca to the ground. He confirms he didn't fully see that. She had shouted something about him hitting or pushing her and she sounded distressed. He saw Rebecca get up and they continued arguing as he and Thierry walked away. 

 76.   He then saw a motion of Keegan hitting Rebecca and her shouting something like, 'Ow, stop hitting me.' When he saw this he and Thierry were already up the road. They carried on walking and turned a corner. A little bit later the car that they had been in drove past them. 

 77.   Mr. Dawson asked some questions. He accepted that he had consumed alcohol throughout the night and he would have been under the influence of it. Most of his memory though is intact. 

 78.   He described how when the vehicle stopped, Keegan and Rebecca got out and Keegan went to the front of the car to investigate the problem. It was at that point that he and Thierry walked off. He said that he was worried about Rebecca as he walked away but he chose not to involve himself. 

 79.   He said that the moon was bright that night and it was clear who was who. He could see who it was who went to, and got up from, the ground. 

 80.   He said that it is possible that Rebecca went to the ground through her intoxication. He confirms that he did see a motion of Keegan hitting, Keegan had his phone torch on whilst this happened. It looked as though Keegan hit Rebecca and it was the motion of what he saw and what Rebecca said that led him to believe that Keegan hit her. Rebecca said,  'Ow, stop hitting me.' He says he doesn't involve himself in other people's problems. 

 81.   Andre Bak gave evidence. He was the CID supervisor in December 2025 and attended Rebecca Caesar Crowie's House in Deadwood on the 27 th of December 2025. He noticed her facial injuries. She had a bust top lip, that was on the inside of the lip, the bottom lip was swollen and she had swelling to her right eye and the bridge of her nose. There was also a cut to the arm and he advised her to go to hospital in relation to that. He then took the photographs of her facial injuries and later conducted the ABE interview. 

 82.   He was asked some questions by Mr. Dawson and clarified that the inside of her top lip was cut and there was swelling to that lip. In terms of when his statement was made he says it wasn't made until the 21st of February 2026 because he thought he had already made one. 

 83.   DC Corker then gave evidence and confirmed that it wasn't until the 25th of February 2026 that Mr Thomas was arrested, he had been wanted by the police since the 27th of December 2025. After his arrest he was interviewed. A transcript of that interview was read to the court. I will not rehearse what was said in the interview in this ruling but I will take the contents of the interview fully into account when making my decision. 

 84.   Mr Dawson then asked him questions. DC Corker said that when he put to the defendant in interview that Rebecca had broken the window whilst trying to get out of the property he had been confused. He now accepts that it was broken whilst getting into the property. 

 85.   Admissions were then read to the court which included the bad character I ruled could be admitted. That was the close of the prosecution case. 

 86.   The defendant gave evidence. He said that on the 26th of December he was at his home address with Rebecca. He said that he's in a relationship with Rebecca and the car belongs to him. He said that on the 26 th he drove Rebecca into town for work but on the way there they got a flat tyre. This led to him and Rebecca walking into town. He then got some help and was able to replace the tyre on the car. 

 87.   The plan was to collect Rebecca from work and so he drove into town sometime between 10 and 11. Rebecca had asked him to bring a bottle of wine down from her house. He met her in town and they went to Kayleigh's house. Rebecca started to drink the bottle of wine in the car and by the time they had got to Donny's she had finished it. 

 88.   At Donny's she had some shots and gin and was drunk by the time they left the bar. They then went to the seafront where her brother and his friend were. They didn't stay long and he, Rebecca, Mickshane and his friend got into the car. The intention was to take Mickshane and his friend home and then he and Rebecca were going to go to her uncle's house as they usually do. 

 89.   When the car got Seaview it cut out. He said it was a dark night. He looked under the bonnet and couldn't see anything wrong. As he closed the bonnet the car started to roll backwards down the hill. By this time the other two boys had got out and walked off towards town. 

 90.   When the car started to roll Rebecca was outside it. He said he saw her let the handbrake off but has no idea why she did that. He chased the car, turned the wheel and pulled the handbrake up causing the car to stop. He asked Rebecca why she did that and she said that the car was no good. Mr Thomas said he then pushed the car out from where it was and trip started it. When he did this he and Rebecca were in the car. He had to turn the car around to carry on the journey back to Deadwood. He said Rebecca got angry as she initially thought he was taking her back to town. 

 91.   He said that Rebecca wanted to drive the vehicle and he had refused to allow her to. When they were at Seaview he said that she grabbed him by the throat with one hand and grabbed the steering wheel with the other, that caused the car to go up a bank. He said he took her hand off his throat, hit the brake and then took her hand off the steering wheel. It was at this stage that her hand accidentally hit her on the lip when he pushed the hand away. 

 92.   They then carried on the journey to Deadwood. They got to Jeremy's house and Rebecca got out of the car first and went inside. When she did this he remained outside smoking a cigarette and putting the windows up on the car. 

 93.   He walked into the house and saw glass on the ground, and then when he saw Rebecca he saw that she had a cut to the arm. Rebecca told him that she had pushed the glass on the door instead of the wood. Mr. Thomas asked her if she wanted to go to hospital and she said she did not want to. He therefore helped her to clean the wound with some toilet roll. 

 94.   After that they sat on the couch and she said they were going to sleep. Rebecca went into the centre bedroom where they always sleep. They had a cigarette, had sex and went to sleep. He confirmed that he did not have to use force to enter the bedroom as the door was already open. 

 95.   He fell asleep and woke up when Rebecca told him that his phone was ringing. He answered the telephone and it was Rebecca's mother. She asked Mr. Thomas if Rebecca was with her and he said yes she was and handed the telephone to her. Rebecca spoke to her mother for about a minute or so, he said that he didn't hear what was said. However after the call Rebecca told her that she needed to go home as her sister was bringing the child back. 

 96.   They got back into the car and Rebecca drove to her mother's house. When they parted Rebecca said that she would ring him later. He said nothing happened on the way back. At Melanie's house they both got out of the car as he was going to drive the vehicle home. 

 97.   Rebecca went inside and her mother came out and accused him of beating Rebecca up. Mr. Thomas told her that she did not hit her. Melanie said that the car was their's so he took the battery out of the car and carried on walking. 

 98.   He clarifies that he didn't threaten Rebecca in the house, she decided to stay there and he did not follow her around. He did not force his way into the bedroom. Rebecca was drunk while at the address. He did not hit her in the vehicle and the injury was caused when he pulled Rebecca's arm away from the steering wheel. He confirmed that Rebecca did not attempt to get out of the car when it was moving and he did not force her into the car. He confirms that he stands by what he says in his interview with the police. 

 99.   Miss Evans then asked some questions. He confirmed that he and Rebecca had been in a relationship for two years and were always together. He normally lives with his mother. His relationship with Bertina Benjamin ended in 2021 or 2022. 

 100.                    He confirmed that he knew Melanie and he has stayed in the house when Melanie was there. However, if the daughter was in the house he would not go inside. He said that Mickshane and Melanie have no problems with him. 

 101.                    He did not know that the evening in Donny's was to celebrate Donny's birthday and he was not aware of any plans for a party the following day. He met Rebecca after work and they went to Kayleigh's. He did not know that Rebecca had left her telephone at Kayleigh's. He said that he would have got to town a little bit before Rebecca finished work. When he went into the house to collect the wine there was nobody at home. 

 102.                    On the journey back home there was music playing and the car broke down at Seaview as it sometimes does when it is hot. When the car stopped the lights dimmed and they turn off when the key is taken out of the ignition. 

 103.                    He looked at the engine and needed to use the light from the screen of his telephone to do so. He said that he was not arguing with Rebecca at this stage, he simply told her that he couldn't see anything wrong. Rebecca was angry that the car had broken down and also because she was not being allowed to drive the car. He then saw Mickshane and Thierry walk down the road. He said that Mickshane did not see what he says he saw and did not hear what he says he heard. 

 104.                    He said he didn't see any injuries to Rebecca's face and does not agree that she had any. He also did not see a nose bleed. He denied assaulting her at Seaview and cannot recall driving past Mickshane and Thierry 

 105.                    He said it was agreed that they would go to Jeremy's house as they always go there when Melanie is at home. He was not planning to take Rebecca to her house and it wasn't the case that he couldn't take her there because of the nosebleed. He confirmed that he knew Jeremy was out that night. He said that Rebecca did not ask to go back to her mother's house. She was not shouting for her mother. It was not at that stage that she tried to grab him, that happened at Seaview. He denied that he had refused to leave her alone at Jeremy's. Rebecca is not right that there was a lock on the bedroom door and in any event they went into the room together. He did not threaten her in the house. 

 106.                    He said the following morning he did not notice any injuries to Rebecca other than when she said that her arm was still hurting. He drove her home in the morning. He said that he knew that the sister had the child from when he had driven Rebecca to work the evening before. 

 107.                    When Melanie came out of the house she was upset. He denies telling her that he had to put his arm across Rebecca to stop her jumping out of the car. He said that she didn't give him a chance to talk, in any event she was more worried about the car. She was angry about Mr. Thomas taking the car away and she only accused him of hitting Rebecca once. He said that since the day of this incident until the time he was arrested he spoke to Rebecca every day. Rebecca told him on that very evening that Melanie had reported the matter to the police. He knew that the police had been looking for him since the 27th of December but said that he did not hide from them. He also said that he was not told that the police were looking for him, it was at that stage that Rick Thomas was threatening to kill him. 

 108.                    He said in his interview that Rebecca had grabbed him by the throat and pulled the wheel. He also said he did tell the police that Rebecca's hand had hit her own face, even though this is not within the transcript. He denies adding that part of his evidence into the account given to this court. 

 109.                    At this point Miss Evans went on to ask Mr. Thomas about his previous convictions. Mr. Thomas refused to carry on answering questions and after a break he returned to the dock. 

 110.                    After discussions with Miss Evans it was clear that she was coming close to the end of her cross examination. She was on her last topic, namely the defendant's previous convictions. After that she was going to put her case to the defendant. I make it clear at this stage that given the defendant was very close to the end of giving his evidence I draw no inference from his failure to carry on answering questions. 

   

   

 Findings on the Evidence 

 111.                    All findings are made to the criminal standard. 

 112.                    I start with the events at Seaview. The prosecution evidence from Miss Caesar Crowie and Mickshane Caesar Crowie is that there was some sort of altercation after the car had come to a halt. Mr Thomas disputes this and denies that he was shouting at Miss Caesar Crowie or that they were arguing. 

 113.                    Miss Caesar Crowie said that as she was walking down the hill Mr Thomas chased her and punched her to the face a couple of times. Mickshane Caesar Crowie describes an argument and seeing Mr Thomas push or pull Miss Caesar Crowie to the floor. Shortly after that he saw a punching motion from the defendant towards Miss Caesar Crowie and heard her shout something like, 'Ow, don't hit me.' 

 114.                    Mr Thomas says simply that did not happen and the only incident at the roadside was when Miss Caesar Crowie let the handbrake off the car. 

 115.                    Miss Caesar Crowie asserts that after she was assaulted outside the car Mr Thomas would not let her continue the walk back to town but instead pulled her inside the car. When inside the car Mr Thomas then punched her to the nose causing it to bleed. In her ABE Miss Caesar Crowie described the motion used by Mr Thomas when he hit her. 

 116.                    Mr Thomas denies that this happened saying that if Miss Caesar Crowie did receive a hit to the face it was when he was trying to remove her hands from the steering wheel and his throat when they were driving. He explains this by saying when he removed her hand from the steering wheel her own arm flew up and hit her in the face, which would not account for the number of injuries sustained. 

 117.                    I am satisfied to the criminal standard that the prosecution version of events is correct in that there was an assault by Mr Thomas upon Miss Caesar Crowie. The complainant's evidence about what happened outside the car is backed up by her brother and there is nothing that undermines that evidence save for the defendant's version of events. Miss Caesar Crowie came by injuries at some point that evening, she did not have them when she got into the car as Mickshane would have seen them, and she had them when she got home the next day. The entire time from leaving town to returning to her mother's the next day Miss Caesar Crowie was in the defendant's company yet he says he never saw the injuries, which I find has been disproved by the prosecution to the criminal standard given that they were obvious. 

 118.                    In light of this I also find that the evidence of Miss Caesar Crowie and Mickshane Crowie that there was an assault is further corroborated by the injuries that the complainant suffered that night and the defendant's propensity to commit offences of assault against those he is in a domestic relationship with. Consequently it follows that the defendant's version of events has been disproved by the prosecution to the criminal standard.  

 119.                    I further find that the assaults were unlawful and intentional, and that the injuries that Miss Caesar Crowie suffered that night were as a result of the assaults. 

 120.                    Miss Caesar Crowie said that there was no intention to stay at Uncle Jeremy's house on that evening with Mr Thomas but that she intended to stay at her mother's house where she also lives. The prosecution led evidence that Miss Caesar Crowie's child was not at home which would have allowed Mr Thomas to remain at the property overnight and that the following day there were plans to decorate the house for Donny's birthday party. Additionally Miss Caesar Crowie said that if the child was not at home then Mr Thomas would normally stay at her house even if her mother was at home. Mr Thomas also accepted that he knew the child was away that night. 

 121.                    This evidence was not challenged save by Mr Thomas saying that they always stayed at Jeremy's house. I find the prosecution have proved to the criminal standard that there was no intention for Miss Caesar Crowie to stay away from home that night, there was simply no reason for her to do so. 

 122.                    During the journey Miss Caesar Crowie asserts that she was asking to go home and that when they got to her house Mr Thomas sped up and drove past it. She said that she tried to get out of the car as it was moving and that she may have grabbed the steering wheel. 

 123.                    Mr Thomas denies this assertion saying that the journey was not unusual except that Miss Caesar Crowie grabbed the steering wheel and also had him by the throat when the car was at Seaview. After he told her that if she did that again she could walk he said that this did not re-occur. 

 124.                     I have found that at Seaview Mr Thomas assaulted Miss Caesar Crowie. Following on from the assault I am satisfied that he made Miss Caesar Crowie get back into the car as the evidence from Mickshane and Miss Caesar Crowie is clear that she was walking away from the car and that she was assaulted as she was doing so. Miss Caesar Crowie had good reason not to get back into the car with Mr Crowie, the car had broken down, she was walking away from it and Mr Thomas had just assaulted her. Additionally Miss Caesar Crowie's account of trying to get out of the moving car is corroborated by the evidence of her mother that Mr Thomas told her that he had had to stop her jumping out. Mr Thomas denies that he said this but it was a clear recollection of Mrs Crowie and not something she can be mistaken about. 

 125.                    Having been made satisfied that Mr Thomas forced Miss Caesar Crowie into the car, that there was no reason to go to Jeremy's house and that there was no plan for the two of them to spend the night at Jeremy's I am satisfied that the defendant took Miss Caesar Crowie to her uncle's house against her will, as further evidenced by her attempt to exit the car while it was moving. 

 126.                    Once at the house Miss Caesar Crowie says that she was detained in that the defendant refused to let her leave and that he would enforce that using threats of assault. Mr Thomas denies this however I have found that he took Miss Caesar Crowie against her will to the property and I am further sure that Miss Caesar Crowie's version of events of what occurred in the house is correct.
